question: Megakernels: fuse the whole forward pass, or delete the idea?

sides.position: Deleted theirs. CUDA Graphs plus PDL recover 98% of the gain, and a megakernel bakes in one model shape and one chip, which breaks as soon as either changes.
Shipping agent-written fused decode paths now, with merged pull requests and gains of 1.3 to 2x over the stock engine.

settles_when: Someone runs the same model on the same chip on AgentX with a fused path against a CUDA Graphs plus PDL path, or either camp changes course.
lean: Possibly both are right. A megakernel's cost was that people had to maintain it. If agents regenerate it per model in a day, the rigidity matters less. Watch whether the fused paths survive the next model release.

question: Does accumulated knowledge make the optimising agents better, or worse?

sides.position: Worse. A curated knowledge base cut the final speed-up by about 19%, and expert-written strategies lost to a one-line instruction by about 26%.
Better. A persistent knowledge base is the agent's policy; a skills library raised the ceiling in ablation; search traces train the next model.
Both. Chains that inherit their own reports climb further, and also carry wrong conclusions forward.

settles_when: A second team publishes an ablation of machine-accumulated (not hand-curated) memory on a production-scale task.
lean: The split may be between knowledge people wrote down, which hurts, and knowledge the loop accumulated and can re-test, which helps until it carries an error. That distinction is the whole of the RSI question in miniature.

question: Is this a job for agents, or for plain search?

sides.position: With the same budget, a simple hyperparameter search beat every agent. Agents know the techniques but explore one configuration and stop.
The gains came from new code (kernel fixes, fused paths) that no search over existing knobs could reach.

settles_when: A benchmark separates gains from configuration and gains from new code on the same task, or InferenceBench runs a matched-budget search next to the newest agents.
lean: Both, at different layers. Knobs belong to search; kernels and engine paths belong to agents. The strongest systems already combine them: Together prunes parallelism layouts with a cost model before any agent runs.

question: Is the moat the traffic, or just the harness?

sides.position: You need real traffic. Synthetic inputs mislead the agents, and nobody can yet simulate traffic they have not seen.
A public set of replayable traces was enough for an academic group with no customers to top the scoreboard.

settles_when: A stack tuned only on the public benchmark is deployed on real traffic and someone reports whether the gains hold.

question: Does specialisation stop at the workload class, or go down to each customer?

sides.position: Class level is most of it. Per-customer tuning was worth about 20% like for like, the recipe transferred to other customers, and a general engine came within 6% of a bespoke one.
Per deployment, continuously. A bespoke engine now costs a couple of hundred GPU-hours, and one company running the loop on its own traffic reports gains at every layer.

settles_when: A provider publishes per-customer against class-level numbers on the same endpoints.

question: Choose the model once per session, or for every request?

sides.position: Once, at the start, or only where no cache is lost: session start, compaction, sub-agent launch. Switching mid-session re-reads the whole context at full price.
Every request or turn, with the cost of the cache miss priced into the decision. A session that gets harder should not be stuck on the model it started with.

settles_when: An independent agentic benchmark with caching priced in compares the two on the same tasks. One early result has a trained per-step router halving cost.
lean: Toward cache boundaries. The team that tried per-request routing and published why moved away from it, and nine-tenths of agent tokens are cached re-reads.

question: Is a router worth building, or is a good default model enough?

sides.position: Routing cuts cost by 30 to 60% at equal quality, by their own measurements.
No router beat always calling a cheap strong model, several collapsed to one model, and a fixed open model already tied a frontier one at two-thirds the cost.

settles_when: A vendor publishes its router against the best fixed model in its own pool, on tasks someone else chose.

question: Tune a model for the job, or wait for the next general one?

sides.position: Tune. On a narrow job it has nearly doubled quality at flat cost, or cut latency by an order of magnitude against a general model.
Wait. A newer general model beat a freshly tuned one on the tuner's own benchmark, a frontier lab is ending self-serve tuning, and a tune dies with its base model.

settles_when: A tuned model is followed against each new general release on the same task for six months.
lean: It depends on how narrow the job is. The wins are on single tasks with their own data and grader; the losses are on general coding, where the next release moves fastest.
